mappings.note: Objects are dropped one by one and the sound noted, which is carrying out the activity and recording what is observed. The conclusion that metals are sonorous is drawn elsewhere; here the observation is the task.

The metal spoon heats through and the wooden one does not, which is exactly the conductors-and-insulators-of-heat differentiation named in LO-34. Not LO-38, because the item contrasts two materials rather than describing the mode of transfer.

Three bottles varying air and water, with the brown deposit recorded for each: a controlled investigation with a results table. Not LO-37, because the item asks for the observations, not yet the cause.

Burn the magnesium, dissolve the ash and test the solution with both litmus papers: an experiment whose observations are being recorded. Not LO-39, because the item asks for the litmus effect rather than for the equation.

Aluminium is chosen for food packaging because it is cheap and easily folded into sheets: a property put to everyday use. Not LO-34, because no two materials are contrasted; a use dictates the choice.

Sodium is picked out from copper, aluminium and zinc by how it reacts with water, a discrimination on a chemical property. Not LO-37, because the item names the metal rather than explaining the reaction.
Why only some metals suit jewellery draws the line from properties such as lustre, malleability and resistance to corrosion to an everyday use.
Matches five everyday uses, from wiring to water purification, to the metal or non-metal behind each. The item is built entirely on uses, so LO-45 rather than LO-33.

Requires the reactions of magnesium and of sulfur with oxygen (LO-39, which names word equations for such reactions) and then the contrast between a basic and an acidic oxide (LO-34). Both halves are asked for.
Completing a flow chart is the flow-chart half of LO-41.

Choosing copper from a mixed list to make a pan for boiling water is applying conductivity and durability to a household object. Not LO-34, because the item asks for a decision and its justification, not for two materials to be separated.
The statements to be judged turn on whether copper is prized for conducting heat or electricity and similar property claims, so the item rests on telling the properties of materials apart.

The oiled nail survives because the film keeps air and water off the iron, which is preventing corrosion, named verbatim in LO-45. Not LO-36, because nothing is set up or recorded; the outcome is predicted.
Asks directly how the properties of metals and non-metals decide their everyday uses, the broadest application item in the batch.

Judges whether sulfur could replace zinc as a rust-proofing coat: an evaluation of a corrosion-prevention method. Not LO-34, because the verdict rests on what a protective coating must do, not on sorting the two elements.
Heating makes iron easier to shape, so the smith's practice is traced back to its cause. Not LO-45, because the item asks why heating works rather than which material to use.
Iron as the smith's material for tawas, buckets and farm tools: a metal identified through its everyday products.
The one-mark twin of the ironsmith item: heating softens the iron so it can be hammered. Same cause-and-effect outcome, since the frame offers no closer home for malleability under heat.
Names lustre as the shine seen on metals, an observable feature of appearance. Not LO-34, because no non-metal is set against it here.
Coal, sulfur and wood against copper and iron on lustre and hardness: an explicit two-group contrast, so LO-34.
Mercury identified as the metal that is liquid at room temperature, a material picked out by an observable state.
Sodium and potassium identified as the metals soft enough to cut with a knife.
Names malleability as the property of being beaten into sheets. Property vocabulary tied to what is observed, so LO-33 rather than LO-35, where materials would be sorted into classes.
Silver foil on sweets and aluminium foil round food: the item asks which property these everyday uses exploit, so it is the use-to-property link rather than the bare definition.
Gold and silver identified as the most malleable metals, a material picked out by degree of a property.
Coal and sulfur shatter where metals flatten, which is the brittle-against-malleable contrast.
Wood is placed against both metals and brittle non-metals as neither malleable nor brittle, a three-way discrimination on the same property.
Names ductility as the property of being drawn into wire.
Electrical fittings and wire jewellery are traced back to ductility: a use-to-property item, so LO-45 rather than the definitional LO-33.
Gold identified by the extreme ductility figure of one gram to a two-kilometre wire.
No wires of coal or sulfur because non-metals are brittle rather than ductile: a metal-against-non-metal contrast.
Steel cables in bridges and cranes are explained by strength plus ductility, a property set behind a real use.
Names sonority as the ringing of a struck metal, an observable feature.
School bells and ghungroos as uses that exploit sonority, so this is the use-to-property item rather than the definition of sonority.
Dull thud against ring, coal and wood against a coin: a direct contrast between metals and non-metals on sonority.
Names conduction as the mode by which heat moves through a material, and LO-38 names modes of transfer of heat explicitly. Not LO-34, because no materials are compared.
The metal spoon outheats the wooden one because metal conducts better: the conductor-and-insulator-of-heat contrast again, here in one-mark form.

Metal pans with wooden or plastic handles is conduction and insulation designed into a household object. Not LO-34, because the two materials are already assigned and the item asks why the design is so.
Names the good-conductors-of-electricity class. Category naming, so LO-35 rather than LO-34.

Aluminium foil and iron nails count as conductors because they complete the tester circuit and light the bulb: the reasoning is about what the test shows. Not LO-35, because the item explains the evidence rather than the class.
